{{Short description|Theorem}}
{{Hatnote|Not to be confused with the [[Hermite–Hadamard inequality]].}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Hadamard's inequality''' (also known as '''Hadamard's theorem on determinants'''<ref>{{cite web|accessdate=2020-06-15|title=Hadamard theorem - Encyclopedia of Mathematics|url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Hadamard_theorem#Hadamard.27s_theorem_on_determinants|website=encyclopediaofmath.org}}</ref>) is a result first published by [[Jacques Hadamard]] in 1893.<ref name=MandS>Maz'ya & Shaposhnikova</ref> It is a [[upper and lower bounds|bound]] on the [[determinant]] of a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] whose entries are [[complex number]]s in terms of the lengths of its column vectors. In [[geometry|geometrical]] terms, when restricted to [[real number]]s, it bounds the [[volume]] in [[Euclidean space]] of ''n'' dimensions marked out by ''n'' vectors ''v<sub>i</sub>'' for 1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''n'' in terms of the lengths of these vectors ||''v<sub>i</sub>''||.

Specifically, Hadamard's inequality states that if ''N'' is the matrix having columns<ref>The result is sometimes stated in terms of row vectors. That this is equivalent is seen by applying the transpose.</ref> ''v<sub>i</sub>'',  then
:<math>\left| \det(N) \right| \le \prod_{i=1}^n \|v_i\|.</math>
If the ''n'' vectors are non-zero, equality in Hadamard's inequality is achieved [[if and only if]] the vectors are [[orthogonal]].

==Alternate forms and corollaries==
A [[corollary]] is that if the entries of an ''n'' by ''n'' matrix ''N'' are bounded by ''B'', so |''N<sub>ij</sub>''| ≤ ''B'' for all ''i'' and ''j'', then
:<math>\left| \det(N) \right| \le B^n n^{n/2}.</math>
In particular, if the entries of ''N'' are +1 and −1 only then<ref>Garling</ref>
:<math>\left| \det(N) \right| \le n^{n/2}.</math>
In [[combinatorics]], matrices ''N'' for which equality holds, i.e. those with orthogonal columns, are called [[Hadamard matrices]].

More generally, suppose that ''N'' is a [[complex number|complex]] matrix of order ''n'', whose entries are bounded by |''N<sub>ij</sub>''| ≤ 1, for each ''i'', ''j'' between 1 and ''n''. Then Hadamard's inequality states that

: <math>|\operatorname{det}(N)| \leq n^{n/2}.</math>

Equality in this bound is attained for a real matrix ''N'' [[if and only if]] ''N'' is a Hadamard matrix.

A [[positive-semidefinite matrix]] ''P'' can be written as ''N''<sup>*</sup>''N'', where ''N''<sup>*</sup> denotes the [[conjugate transpose]] of ''N'' (see [[Definite matrix#Decomposition|Decomposition of a semidefinite matrix]]). Then
:<math>\det(P)=\det(N)^2 \le \prod_{i=1}^n \|v_i\|^2 = \prod_{i=1}^n p_{ii}.</math>
So, the determinant of a [[positive definite matrix]] is less than or equal to the product of its diagonal entries. Sometimes this is also known as Hadamard's inequality.<ref name=MandS/><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Różański|first=Michał|last2=Wituła|first2=Roman|last3=Hetmaniok|first3=Edyta|title=More subtle versions of the Hadamard inequality|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=532|pages=500–511|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2017.07.003|year=2017|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Proof==
The result is trivial if the matrix ''N'' is [[singular matrix|singular]], so assume the columns of ''N'' are [[linearly independent]]. By dividing each column by its Euclidean norm, it can be seen that the result is equivalent to the special case where each column has norm 1, in other words if ''e<sub>i</sub>'' are [[unit vector]]s and ''M'' is the matrix having the ''e<sub>i</sub>'' as columns then
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\left| \det M \right| \le 1,</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

and equality is achieved if and only if the vectors are an [[orthogonal set]]. The general result now follows:
:<math>\left| \det N \right| = \bigg (\prod_{i=1}^n \|v_i\| \bigg) \left|\det M\right| \leq \prod_{i=1}^n \|v_i\|.</math>

To [[mathematical proof|prove]] '''(1)''', consider ''P'' =''M<sup>*</sup>M'' where ''M<sup>*</sup>'' is the conjugate transpose of ''M'', and let the [[eigenvalue]]s of ''P'' be λ<sub>1</sub>, λ<sub>2</sub>, … λ<sub>''n''</sub>. Since the length of each column of ''M'' is 1, each entry in the diagonal of ''P'' is 1, so the [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of ''P'' is ''n''. Applying the [[inequality of arithmetic and geometric means]],
:<math>\det P = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \le \left({1 \over n}\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\right)^n = \left({1 \over n} \operatorname{tr} P \right)^n = 1^n = 1,</math>
so
:<math> \left| \det M \right| = \sqrt{\det P} \le 1.</math>

If there is equality then each of the ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub>'s must all be equal and their sum is ''n'', so they must all be 1. The matrix ''P'' is [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]], therefore [[diagonalizable]], so it is the [[identity matrix]]—in other words the columns of ''M'' are an orthonormal set and the columns of ''N'' are an orthogonal set.<ref>Proof follows, with minor modifications, the second proof given in Maz'ya & Shaposhnikova.</ref> Many other proofs can be found in the literature.
